claim: Type 1 pili are expressed from the fim operon.
source: Type 1 pili genes are expressed from the fim operon.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A diagram of the fim operon structure.

claim: Phase variation of the fim switch (fimS) harboring fimA promoter (pfimA) drives expression of type 1 pili.
source: Phase variation of the fim switch (fimS) harboring fimA promoter (pfimA) drives expression.
evidence: Stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the fim operon structure.

claim: FimB and FimE genes express site-specific recombinases that invert the fimS region by binding to inverted repeats.
source: fimB and fimE genes express site-specific recombinases, FimB and FimE, respectively, inverting the fimS region by binding to the inverted repeats (IR).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A diagram.

claim: Type 1 pili consist of several repeating units of the rod protein FimA, two adaptor proteins FimF and FimG, and the tip protein FimH.
source: Type 1 pili consist of several repeating units of the rod protein FimA, two adaptor proteins FimF and FimG, and the tip protein FimH.
evidence: Stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B showing the structure of type 1 pili.

claim: Phase-locked mutants were generated by deleting the 9-bp recognition site for the site-specific recombinases in the left inverted repeat region of the fimS in either ON or OFF orientation.
source: Phase-locked mutants were generated by deleting the 9-bp recognition site for the site-specific recombinases in the left inverted repeat region of the fimS in either ON or OFF orientation by introducing FRT sites resulting in piliated and non-piliated bacteria (see Methods).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C diagram of the genetic modification.

claim: ON mutants express type 1 pili as confirmed by electron microscopy and yeast agglutination assay.
source: ON (left panel) and OFF mutants (right panel). Electron microscopy images, with zoomed in regions (white boxes) marked in inlays, and yeast agglutination assay.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with electron microscopy images and yeast agglutination results.

claim: OFF mutants do not express type 1 pili as confirmed by electron microscopy and yeast agglutination assay.
source: ON (left panel) and OFF mutants (right panel). Electron microscopy images, with zoomed in regions (white boxes) marked in inlays, and yeast agglutination assay.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D with electron microscopy images showing no pili and negative yeast agglutination.

claim: T cell activation is reduced when DCs are stimulated with UPEC ON bacteria compared to OFF bacteria.
source: The activation of ovalbumin (OVA) specific CD4+ T cells (Banchereau and Steinman, 1998), as assessed by CD69 receptor upregulation and CD62L receptor downregulation, was massively reduced when DCs were stimulated with OVA and UPEC ON bacteria, compared to OVA and UPEC OFF bacteria (Figure 1E).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E with flow cytometry data and quantification.

claim: T cell proliferation is strongly decreased when DCs are stimulated with UPEC ON bacteria compared to OFF bacteria.
source: Accordingly, the number of proliferating T cells was also strongly decreased (Figure 1F).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F with CFSE dilution profiles and quantification.

claim: DC differentiation and maturation are only marginally altered upon exposure to UPEC ON.
source: DC differentiation and maturation, read out with surface levels of CD11c and MHCII, respectively, were only marginally altered upon exposure to UPEC ON (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Expression of co-stimulatory molecules CD40, CD80, and CD86 on DCs is substantially decreased after ON stimulation compared to OFF stimulation.
source: We therefore analyzed surface expression of CD40, CD80, and CD86 after ON and OFF stimulation and found substantially decreased levels after ON stimulation (Figure 1G).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G with flow cytometry histograms and quantification.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPECs prevent effective activation of the adaptive immune response by decreasing surface expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs.
source: These data suggest that type 1 piliated UPECs prevent effective activation of the adaptive immune response by decreasing surface expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs and thus restrict their ability to activate T cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: UPEC ON bacteria increase antigen-specific contact times between DCs and naive CD4+ T cells compared to OFF bacteria.
source: We first investigated DC–T cell contacts using live cell microscopy and found that UPEC ON bacteria, compared to OFF bacteria, increased the antigen specific contact times between DCs and naive CD4+ T cells. Even after 6 hr of co-culture, a large fraction of T cells was unable to dissociate from DCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A with quantification of interaction times.

claim: UPEC ON stimulation shifts CD11b integrin to the active conformation compared to UPEC OFF or LPS stimulation.
source: We found that UPEC ON stimulation shifted CD11b to the active conformation when compared to UPEC OFF or LPS stimulation (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B with flow cytometry data and quantification of CD11b activity.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPECs trigger tight adhesion of DCs to serum-coated surfaces.
source: In line with the finding that type 1 piliated UPEC enhanced CD11b activity, ON bacteria triggered tight adhesion of DCs to serum-coated surfaces (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C with adhesion assay images and quantification.

claim: The differential adhesion caused by ON bacteria is lost in β2 integrin knockout DCs.
source: Similar to the stabilized cell–cell contacts, this surface immobilization was integrin mediated, as for β2 integrin knockout DCs the differential adhesion was lost (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C with quantification comparing WT and Itgb2−/− DCs.

claim: ON stimulated DCs show diminished migration in 3D cell-derived matrices compared to OFF stimulated DCs.
source: Next, we performed in vitro migration assays where DCs migrate in 3D cell-derived matrices (Kaukonen et al., 2017) and found diminished migration after stimulation with ON bacteria (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D with migration assay images and quantification.

claim: Fewer endogenous DCs are found inside lymph vessels after stimulation with ON bacteria compared to OFF stimulation in ear crawl-out assays.
source: Here, the ventral halves of explanted mouse ears were repeatedly exposed to either UPEC ON or OFF bacteria during 48 hr. After stimulation with ON bacteria, fewer endogenous DCs were found inside lymph vessels as compared to OFF stimulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E with microscopy images and quantification.

claim: The migration defect in β2 knockout mice is rescued and similar levels of Itgb2−/− DCs migrate into lymph vessels after ON and OFF stimulation.
source: In ears harvested from β2 knockout mice the migration defect was rescued and similar levels of Itgb2−/− DCs migrated into the lymph vessels after ON and OFF stimulation (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E with quantification comparing WT and Itgb2−/− DCs.

claim: The migration speed of ON and OFF stimulated DCs in 3D collagen is indistinguishable.
source: To test if immobilization by hyperactive CD11b is causative for the loss of migration upon UPEC ON stimulation, we measured migration of DCs in 3D collagen gels. Here, DCs efficiently migrate in an integrin-independent manner (Lämmermann et al., 2008) and hyperactive CD11b, which does not bind to collagen 1, should no longer be able to immobilize ON stimulated cells. Indeed, we found that the migration speed of ON and OFF stimulated DCs in 3D collagen was indistinguishable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F with quantification.

claim: Itgb2−/− DCs still express lowered levels of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation compared to OFF stimulation.
source: Itgb2−/− DCs still expressed lowered levels of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation when compared to OFF stimulation (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that downregulation of co-stimulatory molecules does not depend on integrin activation.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F with quantification.

claim: Downregulation of co-stimulatory molecules does not depend on integrin activation.
source: Itgb2−/− DCs still expressed lowered levels of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation when compared to OFF stimulation (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that downregulation of co-stimulatory molecules does not depend on integrin activation.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that Itgb2−/− DCs still show reduced co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation.

claim: ON stimulated Itgb2−/− DCs are weaker inducers of T cell proliferation than OFF stimulated Itgb2−/− DCs.
source: Although Itgb2−/− DCs were less efficient in supporting T cell proliferation in vitro (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) when compared to WT DCs (as reported previously in vivo; Wu et al., 2018), ON stimulated Itgb2−/− DCs were even weaker inducers of T cell proliferation as OFF stimulated Itgb2−/− DCs.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G with quantification.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPEC increase integrin activity on DCs, leading to increased cell–cell and cell–matrix attachment.
source: Taken together, type 1 piliated UPEC increase integrin activity on DCs, leading to increased cell–cell and cell–matrix attachment.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPEC cause prolonged interaction times with T cells and impaired migratory capacity of DCs.
source: This causes prolonged interaction times with T cells and impaired migratory capacity.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPEC target three functional hallmarks of DCs critical for T cell activation: migration to lymph node, physical interaction with T cells, and expression of co-stimulatory molecules.
source: Together, with the above finding of reduced co-stimulatory molecule expression, these data demonstrate that type 1 piliated UPEC target three functional hallmarks of DCs that are critical for the activation of naive T cells: (1) migration to the lymph node, (2) the physical interaction with T cells, and (3) the expression of co-stimulatory molecules.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Both adhesion and migration of Tlr4−/− DCs after stimulation with UPEC ON bacteria follow the pattern of ON stimulated WT cells.
source: We analyzed Tlr4–/– DCs after stimulation with UPEC ON bacteria and found that both adhesion and migration followed the pattern of ON stimulated WT cells (Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A, B with quantification.

claim: CD80 and CD86 expression on Tlr4−/− DCs is still reduced after ON stimulation compared to OFF stimulation.
source: Importantly, CD80 and CD86 expression was still reduced after ON stimulation when compared to OFF stimulation (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C with quantification.

claim: Receptors other than TLR4 serve as molecular targets of type 1 pili.
source: Therefore, our results, together with recent findings in Salmonella (Uchiya et al., 2019), suggest that other receptors besides TLR4 serve as molecular targets of type 1 pili.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that Tlr4−/− DCs still show the phenotype after ON stimulation, combined with citation to Salmonella findings.

claim: Both DC adhesion and migration functions are fully restored in Cd14−/− DCs stimulated with UPEC ON and OFF bacteria.
source: We performed adhesion and crawl-out migration assays stimulating Cd14−/− DCs with UPEC ON and OFF bacteria, and found that both DC functions were fully restored (Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D, E with quantification.

claim: Cd14−/− DCs show almost full rescue of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation compared to OFF stimulation, with only CD40 still slightly affected.
source: Additionally, Cd14−/− DCs showed almost full rescue of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation, compared to OFF stimulation, with only CD40 still slightly affected (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F with quantification.

claim: TLR4-dependent cytokines IL-6, TNF-α, and CCL5 are not different between ON and OFF stimulated WT DCs.
source: Importantly, TLR4-dependent cytokines, such as IL-6, TNF-α, and the interferon-stimulated CCL5 (Ciesielska et al., 1999), were not different between ON and OFF stimulated WT DCs (Figure 3G) or Cd14−/− DCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3G with quantification.

claim: The absence of CD14 does not inhibit DC activation by bacteria.
source: Thus, the absence of CD14 did not inhibit DC activation by the bacteria and binding of FimH to CD14 did not inhibit the LPS-induced function of CD14 upon exposure to bacteria.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that TLR4-dependent cytokines are not different in Cd14−/− DCs.

claim: Binding of FimH to CD14 does not inhibit the LPS-induced function of CD14 upon exposure to bacteria.
source: Thus, the absence of CD14 did not inhibit DC activation by the bacteria and binding of FimH to CD14 did not inhibit the LPS-induced function of CD14 upon exposure to bacteria.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that TLR4-dependent cytokines are not different between ON and OFF stimulation.

claim: ON bacteria do not inhibit internalization or synthesis of CD14 compared to OFF bacteria.
source: Next, we asked if CD14 endocytosis or canonical CD14 downstream targets were altered upon ON stimulation. We could not detect any interferon-alpha 1 expression, regardless of the bacterial stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) and ON bacteria did not inhibit internalization or synthesis of CD14 when compared to OFF bacteria (Figure 3H).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3H with receptor endocytosis data.

claim: Binding of FimH to CD14 does not alter the signaling capacity of CD14 to drive interferon-dependent responses upon LPS encounter.
source: Given these results, we assume that binding of FimH to CD14 does not alter the signaling capacity of CD14 to drive interferon-dependent responses upon LPS encounter.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that interferon-alpha 1 expression is not detected and CD14 endocytosis is not altered.

claim: UPEC ON bacteria slightly increase CD11b activity on Cd14−/− cells compared to UPEC OFF bacteria.
source: Finally, although integrin activity was reduced in Cd14−/− DCs (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), UPEC ON bacteria still slightly increased CD11b activity on Cd14−/− cells when compared to UPEC OFF bacteria, showing that as opposed to downregulated co-stimulators, integrin activation did not strictly depend on the presence of CD14.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 3I with quantification.

claim: Integrin activation does not strictly depend on the presence of CD14.
source: Finally, although integrin activity was reduced in Cd14−/− DCs (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), UPEC ON bacteria still slightly increased CD11b activity on Cd14−/− cells when compared to UPEC OFF bacteria, showing that as opposed to downregulated co-stimulators, integrin activation did not strictly depend on the presence of CD14.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that Cd14−/− DCs still show some increase in CD11b activity after ON stimulation.

claim: In silico protein–protein docking analysis predicts strong binding of −56.98 kcal/mol between FimH and CD14.
source: In silico protein–protein docking analysis predicted strong binding of −56.98 kcal/mol between FimH (PDB: 6GTV; Sauer et al., 2019) and CD14 (PDB: 1WWL; Kim et al., 2005, Supplementary file 1; Supplementary file 3), which is stronger than the −49.81 kcal/mol between FimH and TLR4 (PDB: 3VQ2; Ohto et al., 2012) or the −35.55 kcal/mol for CD48 (PDB: 2PTV; Velikovsky et al., 2007), another FimH receptor (McArdel et al., 2016; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with computational docking analysis results.

claim: The predicted binding between FimH and CD14 is stronger than the binding between FimH and TLR4.
source: In silico protein–protein docking analysis predicted strong binding of −56.98 kcal/mol between FimH (PDB: 6GTV; Sauer et al., 2019) and CD14 (PDB: 1WWL; Kim et al., 2005, Supplementary file 1; Supplementary file 3), which is stronger than the −49.81 kcal/mol between FimH and TLR4 (PDB: 3VQ2; Ohto et al., 2012) or the −35.55 kcal/mol for CD48 (PDB: 2PTV; Velikovsky et al., 2007), another FimH receptor (McArdel et al., 2016; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with computational docking analysis results comparing binding energies.

claim: Binding sites in FimH are located in its N-terminal domain.
source: Binding sites in FimH were located in its N-terminal domain and in CD14 within the central region of the crescent shaped monomer, in an area not overlapping with the LPS-binding region (Kim et al., 2005; Figure 4A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A with protein structure visualization.

claim: Binding sites in CD14 are within the central region of the crescent shaped monomer, in an area not overlapping with the LPS-binding region.
source: Binding sites in FimH were located in its N-terminal domain and in CD14 within the central region of the crescent shaped monomer, in an area not overlapping with the LPS-binding region (Kim et al., 2005; Figure 4A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A with protein structure visualization.

claim: Predicted strong binding of FimH to human CD14 (−55.95 kcal/mol) is conserved in similar regions of both mouse and human CD14 but mediated by different amino acids.
source: Since CD14 of mouse (PDB: 1WWL) and human (PDB: 4GLP; Kelley et al., 2013) have highly similar secondary structures, but differ in their amino acid sequence (Kelley et al., 2013), we performed docking analysis with human CD14. Predicted strong binding of FimH (−55.95 kcal/mol) was conserved in similar regions of both proteins but mediated by different amino acids (Supplementary file 3 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Stated in the text with computational docking analysis results for human CD14.

claim: The difference in amino acid sequence between mouse and human CD14 is negligible for the conserved binding between FimH and CD14.
source: This indicates that the difference in amino acid sequence between mouse and human CD14 is negligible for the otherwise conserved binding between FimH of type 1 pili and CD14.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that binding is conserved despite amino acid differences.

claim: E. coli mutants lacking fimH still express type 1 pili which are non-functional.
source: Compared to Salmonella, where FimH is necessary for the biosynthesis of type 1 fimbriae (Zeiner et al., 2012), E. coli mutants lacking fimH still express type 1 pili which are, however, non-functional (Maurer and Orndorff, 1985; Klemm and Christiansen, 1987; Jones et al., 1995).
evidence: Stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: ON ΔfimH mutants still express type 1 pili but lack the ability to agglutinate with yeast.
source: We confirmed that our ON ΔfimH mutants still express type 1 pili but lack the ability to agglutinate with yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A with electron microscopy and yeast agglutination assay.

claim: Abundant ON bacteria bind per CD14-coupled bead, whereas binding of fimH deletion mutants is scarce.
source: Using fluorescence microscopy, we found abundant ON bacteria bound per CD14-coupled bead, whereas binding of the fimH deletion mutants was scarce (Figure 4B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B with microscopy images.

claim: ON bacteria show increased binding to CD14-coupled beads compared to fimH deletion mutants or to ON bacteria binding to uncoupled beads.
source: ON bacteria showed increased binding to CD14-coupled beads when compared to the fimH deletion mutants or to ON bacteria binding to uncoupled beads (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C with flow cytometry analysis and quantification.

claim: Biotinylated CD14 only binds to type 1 pili extracts from ON bacteria, whereas no binding is observed to type 1 pili extracts from ON mutants lacking the FimH protein.
source: Biotinylated CD14 only bound to type 1 pili extracts from ON bacteria, whereas no binding was observed to type 1 pili extracts from ON mutants lacking the FimH protein.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the dot blot assay results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Deleting fimH from UPEC ON bacteria fully rescues the adhesion of DCs compared to stimulation with UPEC ON bacteria.
source: Indeed, deleting fimH from UPEC ON bacteria fully rescued the adhesion and the expression of all co-stimulatory molecules when compared to stimulation with the UPEC ON bacteria (Figure 4E, F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E with quantification.

claim: Deleting fimH from UPEC ON bacteria fully rescues the expression of all co-stimulatory molecules on DCs compared to stimulation with UPEC ON bacteria.
source: Indeed, deleting fimH from UPEC ON bacteria fully rescued the adhesion and the expression of all co-stimulatory molecules when compared to stimulation with the UPEC ON bacteria (Figure 4E, F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F with quantification.

claim: Non-pathogenic ON fimHCFT073 bacteria do not affect adhesion of DCs compared to non-pathogenic E. coli W ON bacteria.
source: However, neither adhesion nor expression of co-stimulatory molecules of DCs was affected after stimulation with the non-pathogenic ON fimHCFT073 mutants as compared to the non-pathogenic E. coli W ON bacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with quantification.

claim: Non-pathogenic ON fimHCFT073 bacteria do not affect expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs compared to non-pathogenic E. coli W ON bacteria.
source: However, neither adhesion nor expression of co-stimulatory molecules of DCs was affected after stimulation with the non-pathogenic ON fimHCFT073 mutants as compared to the non-pathogenic E. coli W ON bacteria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C with quantification.

claim: Only the ON bacteria of UTI89 strongly increase adhesion of DCs, whereas ON bacteria of 536 have only a moderate effect.
source: Interestingly, only the ON bacteria of UTI89 strongly increased adhesion of DCs, whereas ON bacteria of 536 had only a moderate effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D with quantification.

claim: Both UTI89 and 536 ON bacteria decrease expression of CD86 only, but not all co-stimulatory molecules.
source: Additionally, none of the two isolates affected all of the co-stimulatory molecules, but both decreased expression of CD86 only (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F with quantification.

claim: The clinical isolate CFT073 expresses additional virulence factors which act downstream of the FimH–CD14 interaction to modulate the functional hallmarks of the immune response of DCs.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that compared to these two strains, the clinical isolate CFT073 expresses additional virulence factors, which act downstream of the FimH–CD14 interaction to modulate the functional hallmarks of the immune response of DCs.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observation that CFT073 has stronger effects than UTI89 and 536.

claim: Blocking the NFAT pathway partially rescues expression of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation.
source: Since NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) signaling was shown to map downstream of CD14-mediated Ca2+ influx (Zanoni et al., 2009), we used the inhibitor FK506 to block calcineurin prior to stimulation with bacteria. Blocking the NFAT pathway partially rescued expression of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), establishing NFAT as one downstream target of FimH.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4G with quantification.

claim: NFAT is one downstream target of FimH.
source: Blocking the NFAT pathway partially rescued expression of co-stimulatory molecules after ON stimulation (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), establishing NFAT as one downstream target of FimH.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that blocking NFAT rescues co-stimulatory molecule expression.

claim: Several NFAT-target cytokines including IL-3, IL-4, IL-10, and GM-CSF are increased after ON compared to OFF stimulation.
source: Indeed, we found several NFAT-target cytokines to be increased after ON compared to OFF stimulation, with IL-3, IL-4, IL-10, and GM-CSF being most severely affected (Figure 4H), whereas blocking of the NFAT pathway or deletion of CD14 resulted in equal expression of NFAT-target cytokines between ON and OFF stimulation (Figure 4H).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4H with quantification.

claim: Blocking of the NFAT pathway or deletion of CD14 results in equal expression of NFAT-target cytokines between ON and OFF stimulation.
source: Indeed, we found several NFAT-target cytokines to be increased after ON compared to OFF stimulation, with IL-3, IL-4, IL-10, and GM-CSF being most severely affected (Figure 4H), whereas blocking of the NFAT pathway or deletion of CD14 resulted in equal expression of NFAT-target cytokines between ON and OFF stimulation (Figure 4H).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 4H with quantification.

claim: CD14 directly binds FimH on the tip of type 1 pili, leading to overactivation of the NFAT pathway and increased expression of immunomodulatory cytokines.
source: Based on these experimental observations, we propose the following model of interaction between FimH on UPECs and CD14 on DCs (Figure 4I): CD14 directly binds FimH on the tip of type 1 pili, leading to overactivation of the NFAT pathway and increased expression of immunomodulatory cytokines, such as GM-CSF, IL-3, IL-4, and IL-10.
evidence: Model proposed based on the experimental data, shown in Figure 4I schematic.

claim: LPS-induced activation of CD14 is not affected by FimH binding, leaving CD14 endocytosis and expression of proinflammatory cytokines unaltered.
source: LPS-induced activation of CD14 is not affected by FimH binding, leaving CD14 endocytosis and expression of proinflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α, IL-6, and CCL5, unaltered.
evidence: Model proposed based on the experimental data showing no difference in TLR4-dependent cytokines and CD14 endocytosis.

claim: The amino acids responsible for binding mannose are located in the mannose-binding pocket (P1, N46, D47, D54, Q133, N135, D140, and F142) and the tyrosine gate (Y48, I52, and Y137).
source: The amino acids responsible for binding mannose are located in the mannose-binding pocket (P1, N46, D47, D54, Q133, N135, D140, and F142; Supplementary file 4; Hung et al., 2002) and the tyrosine gate (Y48, I52, and Y137; Supplementary file 4; Touaibia et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: The amino acids responsible for mannose binding are highly conserved among pathogenic and non-pathogenic E. coli strains.
source: These residues are highly conserved among pathogenic and non-pathogenic E. coli strains (Figure 5A), whereas other amino acids that affect the flexibility of the FimH protein and therefore facilitate host colonization, were found to be mutated in pathogenic E. coli (Chen et al., 2009; Sokurenko et al., 1998; Kalas et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A with amino acid alignment.

claim: The most important amino acids of FimH predicted to be responsible for binding to CD14 are highly conserved among several different E. coli strains, irrespective of their pathogenicity.
source: Interestingly, the most important amino acids of FimH we predicted to be responsible for binding to CD14 are highly conserved among several different E. coli strains, irrespective of their pathogenicity (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A with amino acid alignment.

claim: All four FimH amino acid mutants (Y48A, R98A, T99A, and triple mutant) are still able to bind to CD14-coupled beads.
source: All four FimH mutants were still able to bind to CD14-coupled beads and only the triple mutant showed a more pronounced decrease in binding (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B with quantification.

claim: The triple FimH mutant shows a more pronounced decrease in binding to CD14-coupled beads compared to single mutants.
source: All four FimH mutants were still able to bind to CD14-coupled beads and only the triple mutant showed a more pronounced decrease in binding (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B with quantification.

claim: Stimulating DCs with FimH amino acid mutants shows partial rescue for co-stimulatory molecule expression levels.
source: Stimulating DCs with the FimH amino acid mutants showed partial rescue for co-stimulatory molecule expression levels (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 5C with quantification.

claim: Not only individual amino acids mediate binding to CD14, but most likely several other amino acids are involved, and the supporting secondary structure of FimH as a whole is important for the interaction.
source: This suggests that not only these individual amino acids mediate binding to CD14, but most likely several other amino acids are involved, and thus the supporting secondary structure of FimH as a whole is important for the interaction.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that single amino acid mutations do not completely abolish binding.

claim: 175 µM D-mannose is not sufficient to block binding of UPEC ON bacteria to CD14.
source: Our experiments showed that 175 µM D-mannose was not sufficient to block binding of UPEC ON bacteria to CD14, whereas 1 mM D-mannose and M4284 at 10 µM were able to inhibit binding of ON bacteria to CD14-coupled beads (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A with quantification.

claim: 1 mM D-mannose is able to inhibit binding of ON bacteria to CD14-coupled beads.
source: Our experiments showed that 175 µM D-mannose was not sufficient to block binding of UPEC ON bacteria to CD14, whereas 1 mM D-mannose and M4284 at 10 µM were able to inhibit binding of ON bacteria to CD14-coupled beads (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A with quantification.

claim: M4284 at 10 µM is able to inhibit binding of ON bacteria to CD14-coupled beads.
source: Our experiments showed that 175 µM D-mannose was not sufficient to block binding of UPEC ON bacteria to CD14, whereas 1 mM D-mannose and M4284 at 10 µM were able to inhibit binding of ON bacteria to CD14-coupled beads (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A with quantification.

claim: The blocking CD14 antibody M14-23 is the most effective at rescuing expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs among all tested components.
source: The blocking CD14 antibody reduced bacteria binding to beads by roughly 25% but was the most effective at rescuing expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs among all tested components (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B with quantification.

claim: Existing FimH antagonists and blocking CD14 antibodies interfere with the immunomodulatory action of type 1 piliated pathogens and might be candidates for treating recurring or persistent infections.
source: Thus, existing FimH antagonists as well as blocking CD14 antibodies interfere with the immunomodulatory action of type 1 piliated pathogens and might be candidates for treating recurring or persistent infections.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that antagonists and antibodies can rescue DC function.

claim: Proliferation of T cells is strongly enhanced when DCs are treated with 20 µg/ml M14-23 while stimulated with UPEC ON bacteria compared to ON stimulation only.
source: Proliferation of T cells was strongly enhanced when DCs were treated with 20 µg/ml M14-23, while stimulated with UPEC ON bacteria as compared to ON stimulation only (Figure 6C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C with CFSE dilution profile and quantification.

claim: The interaction of FimH with CD14 is clearly linked to the ability of DCs to mount a functional adaptive immune response.
source: This confirms the importance of CD14 in the interaction of type 1 piliated UPEC with DCs, and clearly links the interaction of FimH with CD14 to the ability of DCs to mount a functional adaptive immune response.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that blocking CD14 rescues T cell proliferation.

claim: Priming of T cells by ON stimulated DCs leads to significantly fewer T cells in late divisions resulting in a reduced proliferation index in vivo.
source: We observed that the same fraction of T cells entered cell division when compared between ON and OFF stimulation. However, priming of T cells by ON stimulated DCs led to significantly fewer T cells in late divisions resulting in a reduced proliferation index, reminiscent of our in vitro findings (Figure 7A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A with CFSE dilution profile and quantification.

claim: Fewer ON compared to OFF stimulated DCs are found inside lymph vessels in individual crawl-in assays.
source: In line with our previous results, we found fewer ON compared to OFF stimulated DCs inside the lymph vessels (Figure 7B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 7B with quantification.

claim: Only slight reduction in the number of ON stimulated DCs in the lymph nodes compared to OFF stimulated ones is observed in individual in vivo migration assays.
source: Interestingly, we observed only slight reduction in the number of ON stimulated DCs in the lymph nodes compared to OFF stimulated ones (Figure 7C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 7C with quantification.

claim: Antibody-mediated blockage of CD14 fully restores migration of ON stimulated DCs in vivo.
source: Notably, antibody-mediated blockage of CD14 fully restored migration of ON stimulated DCs in vivo (Figure 7D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 7D with quantification.

claim: Non-cell autonomous factors can modulate the effect of piliated bacteria on DC migration.
source: The alleviated effect at later time points, when DCs were exposed to inflamed tissue, indicated that non-cell autonomous factors can modulate the effect of piliated bacteria.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that the effect is reduced at later time points in vivo.

claim: No differences in the migration of ON and OFF stimulated DCs are observed when they are mixed together in crawl-in assays or footpad injections.
source: We therefore mixed ON vs. OFF stimulated DCs, stained with different colors, and then either performed crawl-in assays or footpad injections (Figure 7E, F). Strikingly, we could no longer observe any differences in the migration of ON and OFF stimulated DCs.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 7E, F with quantification.

claim: Differentially stimulated DCs mutually affect their migratory capabilities and average the binary response observed at the single-cell level, most likely due to exchange of immunomodulatory cytokines.
source: This result points toward a strong, non-cell autonomous effect where differentially stimulated DCs mutually affect their migratory capabilities and thus average the binary response observed at the single-cell level, most likely due to exchange of immunomodulatory cytokines (Figure 4H).
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that mixed DCs show no difference in migration.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPECs target the glycoprotein CD14 on the surface of DCs and thereby shut down the migratory capacity of DCs and their ability to interact with and activate T cells.
source: Here, we uncovered that type 1 piliated UPECs target the glycoprotein CD14 on the surface of DCs and thereby shut down the migratory capacity of DCs and their ability to interact with and activate T cells.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: Type 1 piliated UPECs decrease the migratory capacity of DCs by increasing their adhesion to other cells and the extracellular matrix by overactivation of integrins.
source: We found that type 1 piliated UPECs decreased the migratory capacity of DCs by increasing their adhesion to other cells, such as T cells, and the extracellular matrix by overactivation of integrins.
evidence: Summary statement of the findings regarding integrin activation and DC migration.

claim: Overactivation of integrins triggered by type 1 piliated UPECs leads to effective immobilization to the extracellular matrix and decreased turnover of cell–cell interactions.
source: To achieve these migratory and signaling tasks, DCs need to dynamically regulate integrin-mediated adhesion, and we found that overactivation of integrins triggered by type 1 piliated UPECs leads to effective immobilization to the extracellular matrix and decreased turnover of cell–cell interactions.
evidence: Summary statement of the findings regarding integrin overactivation effects.

claim: The fimA-encoded major type V fimbriae of the oral pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis bind CD14 and thereby increase integrin-mediated adhesion by activating CD11b integrin.
source: In analogy, a previous study showed that the fimA-encoded major type V fimbriae of the oral pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis also bind CD14 and thereby increase integrin-mediated adhesion by activating CD11b integrin (Harokopakis and Hajishengallis, 2005).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: The pathogenic potential of UPECs does not seem to be the result of a single defined virulence gene, but rather a combination of effects by several factors.
source: Generally, the pathogenic potential of UPECs does not seem to be the result of a single defined virulence gene, but rather a combination of effects by several factors (Touchon et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: The outer membrane of different clinical isolates displays a wide diversity in protein composition.
source: For example, the outer membrane of different clinical isolates displays a wide diversity in protein composition (Wurpel et al., 2015) and the production of outer membrane vesicles delivering associated proteins was linked to pathogenesis (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: The production of outer membrane vesicles delivering associated proteins was linked to pathogenesis.
source: For example, the outer membrane of different clinical isolates displays a wide diversity in protein composition (Wurpel et al., 2015) and the production of outer membrane vesicles delivering associated proteins was linked to pathogenesis (Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: The UPEC strain CFT073 carries accessory genes encoded by 13 pathogenicity islands.
source: Therefore, it remains unknown which other pathogenic gene(s) work together with fimH, as the UPEC strain CFT073 carries accessory genes encoded by 13 pathogenicity islands (Lloyd et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Vaccination approaches against FimH showed promising results.
source: Although vaccination approaches against FimH (Eldridge et al., 2021) or non-conventional treatments, such as small mannosides (Schönemann et al., 2019; Mydock-McGrane et al., 2016), showed promising results, treatments of infections caused by type 1 piliated pathogens remains difficult.
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Non-conventional treatments such as small mannosides showed promising results.
source: Although vaccination approaches against FimH (Eldridge et al., 2021) or non-conventional treatments, such as small mannosides (Schönemann et al., 2019; Mydock-McGrane et al., 2016), showed promising results, treatments of infections caused by type 1 piliated pathogens remains difficult.
evidence: Stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: R98 in FimH is important to stabilize the protein–ligand interaction.
source: For example, R98, showing the strongest binding to CD14 in our predictions, was identified to be important to stabilize the protein–ligand interaction (Han et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Targeting R98 only was not sufficient to boost affinity of FimH antagonists.
source: However, targeting this residue only was not sufficient to boost affinity of FimH antagonists (Tomašič et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Blocking CD14 antibodies such as the human anti-CD14 antibody IC14 could represent an alternative way to treat recurring infections caused by type 1 piliated pathogens.
source: Blocking CD14 antibodies, such as the human anti-CD14 antibody IC14 (Axtelle and Pribble, 2001), could represent an alternative way to treat recurring infections caused by type 1 piliiated pathogens, such as UTIs or inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease (Sivignon et al., 2017), given that CD14 is expressed by hematopoietic but also non-hematopoietic cells (Zanoni and Granucci, 2013).
evidence: Stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: CD14 is expressed by hematopoietic but also non-hematopoietic cells.
source: Blocking CD14 antibodies, such as the human anti-CD14 antibody IC14 (Axtelle and Pribble, 2001), could represent an alternative way to treat recurring infections caused by type 1 piliiated pathogens, such as UTIs or inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease (Sivignon et al., 2017), given that CD14 is expressed by hematopoietic but also non-hematopoietic cells (Zanoni and Granucci, 2013).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Opportunistic pathogens use type 1 pili to adhere to and invade into host epithelial cells.
source: Opportunistic pathogens use type 1 pili to adhere to and invade into host epithelial cells.
evidence: Stated in the text as a general statement about opportunistic pathogens.

claim: UPECs use type 1 pili to actively manipulate the behavior of innate immune cells, and thus also the adaptive immune response, by direct interaction of FimH and CD14 receptor on DCs.
source: While the cellular invasion represents a de facto passive mechanism for the pathogens to hide from the immune system and to establish persistent or recurring infections, we found that UPECs use type 1 pili to actively manipulate the behavior of innate immune cells, and thus also the adaptive immune response, by direct interaction of FimH and CD14 receptor on DCs.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: Binding of FimH to CD14 overactivates the NFAT pathway leading to expression of immunomodulatory cytokines.
source: Binding of FimH to CD14 overactivated the NFAT pathway leading to expression of immunomodulatory cytokines.
evidence: Summary statement of the findings regarding NFAT pathway activation.

claim: IL-10 acts as an immunosuppressant decreasing the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs.
source: For example, we found increased levels of IL-10 which acts as an immunosuppressant decreasing the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs (Mittal and Roche, 2015), drives differentiation of regulatory T cells (Hsu et al., 2015) and is a hallmark cytokine produced by tolerogenic DCs (Domogalla et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: IL-10 drives differentiation of regulatory T cells.
source: For example, we found increased levels of IL-10 which acts as an immunosuppressant decreasing the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs (Mittal and Roche, 2015), drives differentiation of regulatory T cells (Hsu et al., 2015) and is a hallmark cytokine produced by tolerogenic DCs (Domogalla et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: IL-10 is a hallmark cytokine produced by tolerogenic DCs.
source: For example, we found increased levels of IL-10 which acts as an immunosuppressant decreasing the expression of co-stimulatory molecules on DCs (Mittal and Roche, 2015), drives differentiation of regulatory T cells (Hsu et al., 2015) and is a hallmark cytokine produced by tolerogenic DCs (Domogalla et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: The immunosuppressive effects that type 1 piliated UPECs exert on DCs after the FimH–CD14 interaction are averaged in larger populations by non-cell autonomous effects during mixed infections.
source: Although the immunosuppressive effects that type 1 piliated UPECs exert on DCs after the FimH–CD14 interaction are averaged in larger populations by non-cell autonomous effects during mixed infections, our results underscore the importance of the binary response during pathogen–host interaction at the single-cell level given that early immune response to UPECs can decide on the recurrent fate of the infection (Hannan et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Early immune response to UPECs can decide on the recurrent fate of the infection.
source: Although the immunosuppressive effects that type 1 piliated UPECs exert on DCs after the FimH–CD14 interaction are averaged in larger populations by non-cell autonomous effects during mixed infections, our results underscore the importance of the binary response during pathogen–host interaction at the single-cell level given that early immune response to UPECs can decide on the recurrent fate of the infection (Hannan et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: CD14 is a multifunctional co-receptor of several immune cell types.
source: Moreover, since CD14 is a multifunctional co-receptor of several immune cell types (Zanoni and Granucci, 2013) and type 1 pili are expressed not only by pathogenic but also by non-pathogenic E. coli (Shawki and McCole, 2017; Croxen and Finlay, 1999), our findings add a new layer of complexity to the physiological relevance of type 1 pili – as modulators of the immune response in general and specifically during persistent and recurring infections.
evidence: Stated in the text with citation to previous study.

claim: Type 1 pili are expressed not only by pathogenic but also by non-pathogenic E. coli.
source: Moreover, since CD14 is a multifunctional co-receptor of several immune cell types (Zanoni and Granucci, 2013) and type 1 pili are expressed not only by pathogenic but also by non-pathogenic E. coli (Shawki and McCole, 2017; Croxen and Finlay, 1999), our findings add a new layer of complexity to the physiological relevance of type 1 pili – as modulators of the immune response in general and specifically during persistent and recurring infections.
evidence: Stated in the text with citations to previous studies.

claim: The findings add a new layer of complexity to the physiological relevance of type 1 pili as modulators of the immune response in general and specifically during persistent and recurring infections.
source: Moreover, since CD14 is a multifunctional co-receptor of several immune cell types (Zanoni and Granucci, 2013) and type 1 pili are expressed not only by pathogenic but also by non-pathogenic E. coli (Shawki and McCole, 2017; Croxen and Finlay, 1999), our findings add a new layer of complexity to the physiological relevance of type 1 pili – as modulators of the immune response in general and specifically during persistent and recurring infections.
evidence: Summary statement of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: CD14 is the major co-receptor for lipopolysaccharide detection on mouse dendritic cells.
source: Here, we identified CD14, the major co-receptor for lipopolysaccharide detection, on mouse dendritic cells (DCs) as a binding partner of FimH, the protein located at the tip of the type 1 pilus of Escherichia coli.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The FimH amino acids involved in CD14 binding are highly conserved across pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains.
source: The FimH amino acids involved in CD14 binding are highly conserved across pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Binding of the pathogenic strain CFT073 to CD14 reduced DC migration by overactivation of integrins.
source: Binding of the pathogenic strain CFT073 to CD14 reduced DC migration by overactivation of integrins and blunted expression of co-stimulatory molecules by overactivating the NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T-cells) pathway, both rate-limiting factors of T cell activation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Binding of the pathogenic strain CFT073 to CD14 blunted expression of co-stimulatory molecules by overactivating the NFAT pathway.
source: Binding of the pathogenic strain CFT073 to CD14 reduced DC migration by overactivation of integrins and blunted expression of co-stimulatory molecules by overactivating the NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T-cells) pathway, both rate-limiting factors of T cell activation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The response to pathogenic strain CFT073 binding to CD14 was binary at the single-cell level.
source: This response was binary at the single-cell level, but averaged in larger populations exposed to both piliated and non-piliated pathogens, presumably via the exchange of immunomodulatory cytokines.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The response to pathogenic strain CFT073 binding to CD14 was averaged in larger populations exposed to both piliated and non-piliated pathogens, presumably via the exchange of immunomodulatory cytokines.
source: This response was binary at the single-cell level, but averaged in larger populations exposed to both piliated and non-piliated pathogens, presumably via the exchange of immunomodulatory cytokines.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: The interaction between FimH and CD14 represents a potential target to interfere with persistent and recurrent infections, such as urinary tract infections or Crohn's disease.
source: While defining an active molecular mechanism of immune evasion by pathogens, the interaction between FimH and CD14 represents a potential target to interfere with persistent and recurrent infections, such as urinary tract infections or Crohn's disease.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion.
